field_rule:
Buffalograss is a perennial sod-former that spreads characteristically by ABOVEGROUND stolons rooting at leafy nodes; some botanical treatments also report occasional underground rhizomes, so rhizomes alone must not automatically exclude it. Blue grama typically has curved rooster-comb heads and is tufted or short-rhizomatous, while buffalograss usually has separate male combs and female hard bur-like clusters. Curlymesquite has often visibly hairy stolon nodes and a different three-spikelet fascicle; bermudagrass usually has multiple terminal fingers and both stolons and extensive rhizomes. Compare actual flowering and rooted features rather than identifying from one creeping stem.

Scoring audit 2026-11-13: The alternate one-sided branch answer applies only to the MALE comb-shaped heads. Female buffalograss has distinct hard seed clusters; never infer male spikelet structure from a female photo.

field_rule:
Blue grama usually bears 1–3 long curved terminal eyebrow combs whose spikelets extend nearly to the end. Hairy grama often has dense long hairs and a conspicuously bare terminal rachis projection. Pectinata is generally taller with longer and often more numerous combs but overlaps hairy. Texas grama has several much shorter bristly clustered branches. Sideoats has many short side branches all the way down a long stem. Blue grama can also have SHORT STOUT RHIZOMES or form an open low sod; some low culms bend and root at nodes. A rooted decumbent culm is not automatically a true stolon. Retain tuft, verify an underground stem before selecting rhizome, and use attached curved combs plus mature spikelets for the actual identification.

field_rule:
Compared with blue grama, hairy grama has more conspicuously hairy reproductive parts and a naked projecting rachis tip; blue comb spikelets continue toward the tip. A few hairy grama plants form short surface stolons or a low, rooting patch, even though the primary Hill Country treatment describes the species as tufted and without stolons. FNA also allows the usually pectinate branches to arise digitately at the tip. The 'mat' and 'fingers' answers are conditional visual observations; neither alone distinguishes hairy grama from blue grama or KR bluestem. Verify the naked projecting rachis tip, papillose-based hairs and attached mature spikelets.

field_rule:
Tumble windmillgrass tends to have separated tiers of longer (~5–15 cm) racemes and long awns. C. cucullata tends to have crowded shorter whorls and a swollen short-awned sterile hood. C. virgata often has one terminal feathery fan and a different fertile-lemma hair crown. True ligule: Its ciliate membrane may show a short hair fringe, particularly at the edges. The actual inner membrane is still present even when hairs dominate the field of view. Do not mistake long sheath-mouth hairs for the ligule.

Field-score cross-check (2026-11-13): the multi-whorled shape is diagnostic when visible, but every intact attached branch also carries spikelets on one side; a head with seven or more such branches genuinely fits both one-sided choices. These choices are BROAD patterns shared with other grasses, not permission to name a Chloris species without head-tier spacing and mature spikelets.

field_rule: INLAND SEA OATS — look for large fish-shaped HANGING SPIKELETS on long thin pedicels under broad bamboo-like leaves. Follow the genuine live panicle in Bob Harms CHLA5-I; CHLA5-J isolates ONE actual many-flowered flattened green SPIKELET. Each overlapping pointed shield is a FLORET LEMMA, not one loose grass seed. CHLA5-j1 shows the dry hanging stage, CHLA5-J2 an actual yellowish pollen-bearing ANTHER in an opened floret, CHLA5-9 separates enclosing floral scales and TRUE DARK CARYOPSIS, and CHLA5-8 reveals actual scaly shallow rhizome and attached root crowns. The available images do not independently establish the inner ligule. A rooted tuft is also valid: Hill Country plants are cespitose with short knotty rhizomes. The ciliate ligule has a minute membranous base; a hair-fringed view must not falsely exclude it.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow an actual dangling flat SPIKELET along a thin pedicel
diagnostic_checks.check: Inland sea oats has long-drooping panicle branches and broad, flat fish-shaped spikelets around 20–40 mm in many mature sources (smaller in some southern keys). Each apparent 'scale' is a separate FLORET lemma, not a single giant seed.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Small woodoats (*C. laxum*) tends to have smaller spikelets, stiffer/ascending head branches and much shorter stalks; wild oat grass has a different floret shape and awns.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Missouri DNR/WFO; same-specimen head plus one full isolated spikelet and pedicel needed

diagnostic_checks.look: COUNT the overlapping fertility-bearing lemmas and locate glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: Typically about 6–20 florets in the dramatically flattened spikelet; paired narrow basal glumes and often 1–2 basal sterile lemmas differ from broad many-veined (often 11–15-veined) fertile lemmas. Dark true grain is within lemma + palea, not the whole hanging unit.

diagnostic_checks.certainty: Floret range differs among regional taxon accounts; current gallery crops not dissected/verified
